title: Psychology of Human Relationships Adventure 1: Formation of Relationships
welcome_lead: Today you'll explore why people form relationships — similarity, proximity and reward.
meta_desc: Psychology Human Relationships: similarity-attraction, proximity, reward theory and biological factors.
final_note: You explained three factors in relationship formation and supporting studies.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Donn Byrne (1971): the similarity-attraction effect — we like people who share our attitudes, values and demographics.

Festinger, Schachter & Back (1950): MIT student housing study — residents formed friendships with people on the same floor, especially nearby doors (functional distance).

Reward theory (Byrne & Clore, 1970): we associate people with the rewards we feel in their presence.

Robert Zajonc (1968) mere exposure effect — simply seeing a face repeatedly raises liking.

Both fit a behaviourist conditioning framework.

Wedekind 'sweaty T-shirt' study (1995): women preferred T-shirts of men with dissimilar MHC genes (immune diversity).

Oxytocin: Kosfeld et al. (2005) — intranasal oxytocin raised trust in an economic game (effect debated).

Evolutionary view: humans evolved to seek mates with genetic and parental fitness cues.
